variants.title: Follow the reconciliation loop
variants.context: Kubernetes is declarative: declare desired state, the API server persists and validates it, the scheduler places Pods, kubelets run and observe them, and controllers reconcile again until observed matches desired or progress stops.
variants.prompt: A Deployment is applied. Put the loop in order.

items.text: Controllers replace missing replicas, progress rollouts, update endpoints, and retry until converged.
The API server authenticates, authorizes, applies admission policy, validates, and persists the object.
The scheduler chooses nodes that satisfy resource, affinity, taint, storage, and topology constraints.
Kubelets pull images, start containers, mount configuration and volumes, run probes, and report status.
Declare desired state with identity, replicas, image digest, requests, probes, and rollout policy.

variants.hint: An accepted write is not a ready workload.
variants.explanation: Declare → persist → schedule → run and observe → reconcile again. Reconciliation is asynchronous.

variants.title: Follow the reconciliation loop
variants.context: Kubernetes is declarative: declare desired state, the API server persists and validates it, the scheduler places Pods, kubelets run and observe them, and controllers reconcile again until observed matches desired or progress stops.
variants.prompt: A node dies. Put the recovery in order.

items.text: The API server still holds the declared state.
Controllers keep reconciling until the replicas are ready again.
The scheduler finds nodes for replacement Pods.
Kubelets on those nodes start containers and run probes.
The desired replica count is unchanged in the API.

variants.hint: Desired state does not change when reality does.
variants.explanation: Controllers move reality toward the declaration; users still own what happens to in-flight requests.

variants.title: Follow the reconciliation loop
variants.context: Kubernetes is declarative: declare desired state, the API server persists and validates it, the scheduler places Pods, kubelets run and observe them, and controllers reconcile again until observed matches desired or progress stops.
variants.prompt: An apply returns success but the app is not serving. Put the stages the rollout must still pass in order.

items.text: Pods still need scheduling against real capacity.
Endpoints update only when controllers observe ready Pods.
Containers need to start and pass readiness.

variants.hint: A successful API write means acceptance, not readiness.
variants.explanation: Dependent resources converge later; watch Pending reasons and probe transitions.

variants.title: Pick the object
variants.context: Deployment: stateless rolling replacement. Service: stable discovery of ready endpoints. Job and CronJob: finite work that must tolerate repeats. StatefulSet: ordered identities and per-replica storage. DaemonSet: a node-local agent on every selected node.
variants.prompt: Interchangeable stateless web replicas that roll out with rolling replacement. Which object?
options: Deployment.
StatefulSet.
DaemonSet.
optionFeedback: Deployments own ReplicaSets and roll interchangeable Pods.
StatefulSets are for stable identity and storage.
DaemonSets run per node.

variants.title: Pick the object
variants.context: Deployment: stateless rolling replacement. Service: stable discovery of ready endpoints. Job and CronJob: finite work that must tolerate repeats. StatefulSet: ordered identities and per-replica storage. DaemonSet: a node-local agent on every selected node.
variants.prompt: A database needs ordered identities and per-replica storage claims. Which object, and what does it still not provide?
options: Job; it does not keep data between runs.
StatefulSet; the application still owns replication.
Deployment; it does not give stable identities.
optionFeedback: Jobs run finite work to completion and never hold a stable identity or a storage claim.
Stable identity and storage claims, not database semantics.
Deployments roll interchangeable Pods, so replicas get no stable identity or per-replica volume.
variants.hint: What does stable identity actually guarantee?
variants.explanation: StatefulSet is identity plumbing, not a replicated database.

variants.title: Pick the object
variants.context: Deployment: stateless rolling replacement. Service: stable discovery of ready endpoints. Job and CronJob: finite work that must tolerate repeats. StatefulSet: ordered identities and per-replica storage. DaemonSet: a node-local agent on every selected node.
variants.prompt: A log-shipping agent must run on every node. Which object?
options: CronJob.
DaemonSet.
Deployment with many replicas.
optionFeedback: CronJobs are scheduled, finite work.
DaemonSets place a Pod on each selected node and consume capacity there.
Replica counts do not guarantee one per node.
variants.hint: Where must exactly one copy run?

variants.title: Give each probe one job
variants.context: Startup probes protect slow starts; readiness says whether this Pod should receive traffic now; liveness restarts a process that cannot recover. Probe health alone cannot approve a release; the application SLO can.
variants.prompt: A shared downstream is unavailable and liveness probes restart every healthy replica. What is wrong?
options: The shared downstream should be restarted instead.
Liveness must not restart a Pod because a dependency is down.
Nothing; a restart is cheap and may clear the error.
optionFeedback: Kubernetes restarts containers it schedules, not an external dependency it does not own.
Restarting healthy processes makes an outage worse.
Restart loops throw away warm capacity while the dependency is still down.
variants.explanation: Liveness detects a process that cannot recover without restart.

variants.title: Give each probe one job
variants.context: Startup probes protect slow starts; readiness says whether this Pod should receive traffic now; liveness restarts a process that cannot recover. Probe health alone cannot approve a release; the application SLO can.
variants.prompt: A JVM takes 90 seconds to start and gets killed by liveness at 30 seconds. Which probe fixes this?
options: A startup probe that delays liveness until start.
A readiness probe with a longer initial delay.
Raise the liveness timeout to 120 seconds.
optionFeedback: Startup probes protect slow starts.
Readiness controls traffic only. Liveness keeps its own clock and still kills the process at 30 seconds.
A blanket longer timeout applies for the whole life of the Pod, so a wedged process waits two minutes for every restart.
variants.explanation: Once startup succeeds, normal liveness and readiness begin.

variants.title: Give each probe one job
variants.context: Startup probes protect slow starts; readiness says whether this Pod should receive traffic now; liveness restarts a process that cannot recover. Probe health alone cannot approve a release; the application SLO can.
variants.prompt: All probes pass after a release, but users see errors. Can probe health approve the release?
options: Yes; every probe is green after the rollout.
Yes, provided the readiness check is strict.
No. Measure user outcomes such as success and latency.
optionFeedback: Probes check the process, not what users receive, so green probes coexist with user-visible errors.
A stricter readiness check still tests the same process-level signal, not user outcomes.
Probes are process-level signals.
variants.hint: What do users experience that a probe cannot see?
variants.explanation: Candidate-versus-baseline release metrics with automated rollback thresholds approve releases.

variants.title: Plan the headroom
variants.context: Node capacity is not fully schedulable. Requests reserve; limits throttle or terminate. Size for the failure and rollout overlap you promise to survive.
variants.prompt: Six nodes each have 16 allocatable cores. You must survive one node loss without Pending Pods. How many cores are usable for workloads?
variants.explanation: (6 − 1) × 16 = 80 cores; the sixth node is the failure headroom.

mistakes.feedback: That uses all six nodes with no failure headroom.

variants.title: Plan the headroom
variants.context: Node capacity is not fully schedulable. Requests reserve; limits throttle or terminate. Size for the failure and rollout overlap you promise to survive.
variants.prompt: Pods request 2 cores each and 80 cores are usable. How many Pods can be scheduled?
variants.hint: Divide usable cores by the request.
variants.explanation: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 Pods. Requests, not limits, drive scheduling.

mistakes.feedback: Only 80 cores are usable after headroom.
That multiplies the 80 usable cores by the 2 core request instead of dividing by it.

variants.title: Plan the headroom
variants.context: Node capacity is not fully schedulable. Requests reserve; limits throttle or terminate. Size for the failure and rollout overlap you promise to survive.
variants.prompt: A Deployment has 8 replicas and maxSurge is 25%. How many extra Pods can exist during a rolling update?
variants.hint: Apply the surge percentage to the replica count.
variants.explanation: 25% of 8 is 2 extra Pods, which must fit in headroom during the rollout.

mistakes.feedback: Surge is a fraction of replicas.
That adds the default 25% maxUnavailable as well; only maxSurge creates extra Pods, so 25% of 8 is 2.

variants.title: Separate config, secrets, and data
variants.context: ConfigMaps carry non-secret configuration. Secret objects need encryption, least privilege, rotation, and audit. PersistentVolumeClaims do not create replication, point-in-time recovery, or tested restores. Deploy digests, not mutable tags.
variants.prompt: A PersistentVolumeClaim is bound. Does the database now have replication and point-in-time recovery?
options: Yes; the storage layer keeps redundant copies.
Yes, when the storage class is SSD-backed.
No. A claim requests storage, nothing more.
optionFeedback: Redundant disks survive hardware loss. They do not give point-in-time recovery of the database.
The storage class sets performance, not replication or recovery.
Claims do not create database semantics.
variants.hint: What does a claim actually provide?
variants.explanation: Back up application data and control-plane state independently, then rehearse restores.

variants.title: Separate config, secrets, and data
variants.context: ConfigMaps carry non-secret configuration. Secret objects need encryption, least privilege, rotation, and audit. PersistentVolumeClaims do not create replication, point-in-time recovery, or tested restores. Deploy digests, not mutable tags.
variants.prompt: Manifests reference image tag v2. Why prefer a digest?
options: Digests pull faster from the registry cache.
Tags are not supported by the scheduler.
A digest names the exact artifact deployed.
optionFeedback: Pull speed depends on layers and caching, not on how the image is named.
Tags work fine. The problem is that a tag can be repointed at different bytes.
Mutable tags can move underneath a rollout.
variants.explanation: Avoid mutable image tags; deploy digests.

variants.title: Separate config, secrets, and data
variants.context: ConfigMaps carry non-secret configuration. Secret objects need encryption, least privilege, rotation, and audit. PersistentVolumeClaims do not create replication, point-in-time recovery, or tested restores. Deploy digests, not mutable tags.
variants.prompt: Sensitive bytes live in a Secret object. Is the design complete?
options: No. Add encryption, rotation, audit, and least privilege.
Yes; the Secret keeps the bytes out of the manifest.
Yes, because Secret values are base64 encoded.
optionFeedback: The object is distribution, not a complete secrets design.
Keeping bytes out of a manifest is one step. Access, rotation, and audit are still missing.
base64 is encoding, not protection. Anyone who can read the object can read the value.
variants.hint: Who can read the Secret, and how does it rotate?
variants.explanation: Rotate secrets without exposing them in manifests, logs, or environment dumps.
